A $10,000 investment in NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) made five years ago, on November 3, 2021, has grown to approximately $76,300 by November 2, 2026. In comparison, the same amount invested in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has only increased to about $12,200. This dramatic difference highlights why the Bitcoin vs. Nvidia competition isn’t even close, despite both facing some tough times recently. Bitcoin is trading at $77,609, up 0.4% in the last 24 hours but down 10.4% over the past 30 days. The cryptocurrency reached a high of just over $86,000 on October 4, but it closed at $76,709 on November 2, marking its lowest close in a month. This puts Bitcoin down about 38.4% from its all-time high of $126,080. Is Now The Time To Buy For Alphabet, Microsoft or Nvidia? NVIDIA hasn’t been immune to market pressures either. The company’s stock is currently at $208, up 3.1% on the day, though it has dropped 13.6% over the month leading up to November 2. So, what accounts for such a massive difference between these two investments? To understand Nvidia’s incredible growth, we can look back at its stock price on November 3, 2021, which was $26.48—adjusted for splits. By the close on November 2, 2026, that same $10,000 investment stands at about $76,301, an impressive 663% gain, or about 50.1% per year. In contrast, the $10,000 invested in Bitcoin when it was priced at $63,025 grew to about $12,171 by the same date, a modest 21.7% gain, or roughly 4% annually. In every time frame examined, Nvidia has outperformed Bitcoin. Over a three-year period, Bitcoin posted strong annual growth of about 30.2%, but Nvidia still outperformed at 65.1% per year. Over the last year, Bitcoin holders lost far more value than those who invested in Nvidia. Both Bitcoin and Nvidia fell sharply early in the five-year timeframe. Bitcoin fell dramatically from peak to trough by 76.6%, reaching its lowest point on November 21, 2022. Nvidia, while also affected, fell less, down 66.4% from its November 29, 2021 close to its October 14, 2022 close. After reaching their lows, the trajectories diverged. Nvidia benefited from a strong business model and significant revenue growth. For fiscal 2026, which ended in January 2026, Nvidia reported staggering revenue of $215.9 billion, a 65.5% year-over-year increase, along with net income of $120.1 billion. The company’s most recent quarter showed even stronger performance, with revenue rising to $96.2 billion, a 105.8% increase from the previous year. During the August 26 earnings call, CFO Colette Kress stated, “NVIDIA compute is fully utilized across every cloud we serve.” With non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.22 surpassing the expected $2.09, Nvidia has projected third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and expects revenue to grow around 70% in fiscal 2028. In contrast, Bitcoin lacks a revenue structure; its price is determined solely by market demand. Despite its past peaks, Bitcoin has faced significant volatility since reaching its all-time high, which contributes to its relatively poor performance over the five-year span. Both Bitcoin and Nvidia are now influenced by investor risk sentiment and the rise of AI technology. As noted in Nvidia’s recent call, major cloud companies plan to invest nearly $800 billion in capital projects in 2026 and about $1.3 trillion in 2027, with implications beyond Nvidia. When tech stocks face volatility, Bitcoin tends to decline as well, as seen recently following the Binance hack in late October. Over the last week, Nvidia fell 6.5%, while Bitcoin declined 3.7%. Nvidia has clearly outperformed Bitcoin over the past five years. A $10,000 investment in Nvidia has grown to around $76,300, driven by steady earnings growth, while Bitcoin’s value has reached only about $12,200. Although Bitcoin showed a strong percentage increase over three years because of its lower starting price, its five-year performance is lackluster compared to Nvidia. Both assets still carry risks; if Nvidia’s future earnings reports fall short of expectations, it could create a downward trend for both Nvidia and Bitcoin. title: While the Rest of the Market Focuses on the Anthropic IPO, These Are My Top 2 Stocks to Buy in November - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia and Broadcom are two of Anthropic's primary computing unit suppliers. The biggest stock market news in November will likely be the initial public offering of Anthropic, which is likely to happen sometime before Thanksgiving.  There will be a lot of fanfare and enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic stock when it goes public, but I expect it will eventually fade, much like what happened after Space Exploration Technologies' IPO earlier this year. However, two companies that have strong business relationships with Anthropic look like fantastic investments now: Nvidia (NVDA +2.29%) and Broadcom (AVGO +3.07%). Both stocks look highly attractive, and I think investors should pick up shares of them in November rather than waiting for Anthropic to debut. Nvidia and Broadcom both make AI computing units. Nvidia makes graphics processing units (GPUs), while Broadcom makes custom AI chips. The companies are competing for shares of the same market in data centers, but there is plenty of room for both to succeed, and each chipmaker tackles a different problem. Nvidia's GPUs are the industry standard in AI computing. They work well in nearly every application where heavy parallel processing power is the key requirement, making them highly flexible and repurposable for an array of computationally intense tasks. However, because they're not optimized for any one task, they're less cost-efficient when placed in servers where they'll be handling just one type of workload for their entire lifespan. That's where a custom AI computing unit from Broadcom makes a lot of sense. Instead of offering a flexible, one-size-fits-all chip, it partners directly with hyperscalers to design AI chips that are tailored to their specific workloads. While Anthropic isn't designing its own chips right now, it is using chips co-designed by Alphabet (Google's parent company) and Broadcom. Those Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) can outperform GPUs from a cost perspective on some types of AI workloads, which makes them an attractive choice for Anthropic. Sometimes, it's better to own the supplier's stock rather than the customer's, and I think that's the case here. Broadcom and Nvidia already have an established business with huge profit margins and high growth. With Anthropic, it's more important to remember that not every promising, fast-growing company manages to make the pivot to long-term profitability. Fortunately, both Broadcom and Nvidia are priced pretty attractively right now, making them excellent buys. Nvidia and Broadcom may be the poster children of the AI processor segment, but the market has shown no respect for their 2027 growth prospects. If we utilize next year's earnings projections to value these stocks, they trade at massive discounts to their current trailing price-to-earnings ratios. The question is, what is a fair P/E ratio to pay for these two? I think something like 30 times trailing earnings is a fair price to pay. So, if Nvidia hits its earnings projections for next year, the stock could rise by over 100%. For Broadcom to trade at that level a year from now, it would have to almost double. Those are returns that are staring investors in the face, while there is far less clarity about what Anthropic's future might look like. Broadcom and Nvidia look well positioned to have huge years in 2027, and their shareholders don't face the types of risks that come with investing in a newly public company. As a result, I think Broadcom and Nvidia are the two best stocks to buy in the market in November, and investors shouldn't wait around too long to take advantage of their low prices, as they could start to soar as the market looks ahead to 2027. content: A startup CEO backed by NVIDIA just called Chinese open-source AI models a Trojan horse for Chinese chips, yet semiconductor investors shrugged off the warning and sent chip stocks higher anyway. Here is what explains the disconnect. A warning that Chinese AI labs could soon sell chips abroad isn’t keeping buyers away from NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction). NVIDIA stock traded at $208.24 in the afternoon, up 3% from Monday’s close of $202.06. The gain snaps a four-session losing streak. Even so, NVIDIA stock remains down 11% over the past month. Misha Laskin, CEO of NVIDIA-backed startup Reflection AI, warned in comments reported November 3 that Chinese AI labs giving away open models abroad will start selling their own hardware alongside them. Laskin called open models “Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring.” Chinese companies selling open models into the Middle East, other Asian countries or Brazil “will now also start selling chips and their data centers,” he said. That’s a challenge aimed directly at NVIDIA’s ecosystem. NVIDIA has already removed China from its forecasts. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress said on the company’s August 26 earnings call, “Given ongoing geopolitical uncertainty, there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook.” China revenue, including Hong Kong, fell to $19.7 billion in fiscal 2026 from $25.0 billion the prior year. What Laskin describes hits a different pool: NVIDIA’s sales outside both the U.S. and China, where sovereign AI revenue grew 35% sequentially in Q2 FY2027. The valuation helps explain why buyers shrugged off both items. At 17x forward earnings, NVIDIA trades at a five-year low, versus a five-year average of 36x. Supply is the other buffer, with CEO Jensen Huang telling analysts in August, “Even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%.” Such a gap suggests Chinese hardware competition may weigh more on NVIDIA’s growth beyond fiscal 2028 than on near-term sales. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is at $491.87, up 5%, the strongest gain among the three. Q3 2026 results from AMD arrive after the close on November 3, offering a near-term read on AI chip demand ahead of NVIDIA’s own report. Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) stock is at $332.63, up 3%, running a step ahead of NVIDIA. With all three chip names rising together, NVIDIA’s move looks like part of a sector-wide recovery. NVIDIA sells graphics processing units (GPUs), central processing units (CPUs), networking gear and software as one platform that runs in every major cloud. Huang framed it on the August call: “NVIDIA is a platform, an entire AI factory platform that spans the entire AI life cycle, that you can use in any cloud.” AMD competes as a merchant alternative for GPUs and server CPUs, while Broadcom builds custom accelerators and networking chips designed around individual hyperscalers’ needs. That breadth shapes how NVIDIA meets the threat Laskin described. On the same call, Huang said, “Nearly all open models run on NVIDIA, and the reason for that is because NVIDIA’s footprint around the world is the highest, and our architecture is the most fungible.” Chinese labs matching their own chips with open models would be competing for that same global footprint. NVIDIA has scheduled its Q3 FY2027 results for November 17, and the company guided for revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. The next test for NVIDIA is whether management describes demand outside the U.S. and China as holding firm against bundled Chinese offerings. The bull case rests on a forward multiple at a five-year low and NVIDIA’s demand that still exceeds supply. The bears see a risk that Chinese models, chips and data centers sold as a package could erode NVIDIA’s position in the Middle East, Asia and Latin America over time. title: AI CEO Warns Chinese Labs Will Use Free Models to “Start Selling Chips” Against Nvidia - TIKR.com
content: sasha85ru from Getty Images, Jordan Harrison from Pexels China’s AI labs keep giving away some of the best models in the world, and one AI CEO says the real business is what gets sold alongside them. That’s a problem for NVIDIA (NVDA), whose stock is already down 11% in the past month. Misha Laskin, co-founder and CEO of Reflection AI, a startup building American open models to compete with China’s, called open models “Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring” on the latest episode of Prof G Markets. The model is only the engine, he said: “You need the car around it. And what’s the car? Well, it’s the chips, right?” And Laskin expects China to sell the car abroad: “when Chinese companies go and sell open models into the Middle East or other Asian countries or Brazil or what have you, they will now also start selling chips and their data centers.” He was making a national security point, warning that allied nations “will start getting locked into Chinese infrastructure.” For NVIDIA shareholders, it’s a sales problem too. TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Nvidia. How many say “Buy”? See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street’s revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia’s Analyst Ratings NVIDIA has all but written China off. Its revenue from China, Hong Kong included, fell to $19.7 billion in fiscal 2026 (the year ended January 2026) from $25.0 billion. In the July quarter, H200 sales there were less than 1% of its $89 billion of data center revenue. CFO Colette Kress told analysts that “there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook.” Laskin is talking about everywhere else. Customers based outside the US and China brought in about a fifth of NVIDIA’s fiscal 2026 revenue. That’s the business a free model bundled with chips would go after. Analysts expect that business, and the rest of NVIDIA’s, to keep growing fast. They see revenue more than quadrupling, from $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026 to $903 billion in fiscal 2029: Chinese models are close behind the best American ones. Ramez Nam ran the numbers and found that Moonshot AI’s Kimi “is now about five weeks behind the U.S. frontier,” Peter Diamandis said on his Moonshots podcast. The newest Kimi model costs a third of what the last one did, and Moonshot plans to release its weights for anyone to run. Chinese chipmakers are catching up, too. Peter Tchir, head of macro strategy at Academy Securities, said on Bloomberg Surveillance last week that “we’ve been talking a lot at Academy Securities about the potential for cheap Chinese compute to come on the market. And we feel that’s one of the biggest threats.” Cheap is the word NVIDIA has to worry about. Its gross margin, the clearest sign of its pricing power, rose from 56.9% in fiscal 2023 to 75.0% in fiscal 2025, then eased to 71.1% in fiscal 2026: Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in the January 2027 quarter as memory costs climb. That’s before any cheaper Chinese bid turns up in a government’s data center deal. NVIDIA has one big cushion: it can’t make enough chips. In August, management told analysts it expects revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028, and said supply is what limits that number. I’d bet a sovereign deal lost in the Gulf today just frees up racks for the next buyer in line. NVIDIA would feel it later. Analysts already expect revenue growth to slow from 68.2% in fiscal 2028 to 30.5% in fiscal 2029, and by then I’d expect buyers abroad to have more chips to choose from. If Laskin is right about lock-in, any government NVIDIA loses then will be hard to win back. Investors already expect a sharp slowdown. NVIDIA trades at 17x forward earnings, its lowest in five years and less than half its 36x average: Laskin’s playbook makes sense: give away the engine, sell the car. China’s labs already have the models, and Tchir thinks its chipmakers are catching up. The way I see it, that threatens NVIDIA’s growth after fiscal 2028 and its margins. At 17x forward earnings, investors are already paying very little for those years. So for me, the drop looks like an opportunity. Of course, Laskin is describing what he expects Chinese labs to do. What would change my mind is a Chinese lab winning a government deal abroad with its own chips in the package. NVIDIA sells the whole AI toolkit: chips, networking, CUDA software and full systems. The biggest AI buyers keep signing on for multiple product generations. OpenAI committed to 10+ gigawatts of NVIDIA systems, Anthropic is taking up 1GW, and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) signed a multi-year, multi-generation agreement. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $2.22 vs. the $2.09 consensus, the 5th consecutive beat. Management guided Q3 revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. Second, the valuation got cheaper while profits rose. NVIDIA’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, put it plainly: “AI has reached its inflection point. It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. title: NVDA Stock Rebounds Off $200 Support after Nvidia CEO Comments and Anthropic Expansion - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares have recovered approximately 3% after retreating toward $200, as improving geopolitical sentiment supports technology stocks, while Big Tech earnings, rising infrastructure costs, custom-chip competition and financing risks continue to challenge the semiconductor sector Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares have struggled to maintain their upward momentum after retreating from record highs above $243, falling toward $200 as disappointing Big Tech earnings and concerns about infrastructure spending weighed on semiconductor stocks. The stock recently recovered toward $220 after finding support around $210, but the rebound lost momentum as investors reassessed the sustainability of technology companies’ enormous infrastructure commitments. Nvidia is now attempting another recovery, gaining approximately 3% as improving sentiment surrounding the Middle East conflict supports broader market sentiment. Comments from President Trump during a Fox News interview concerning Israel and the conflict with Iran have encouraged expectations that Washington could pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran. The prospect of de-escalation has also contributed to downward pressure on oil prices, helping improve sentiment across financial markets. However, the broader semiconductor outlook remains complicated. Strong demand for processors and memory does not necessarily guarantee continued earnings growth, particularly when customers must secure financing, electricity and operational capacity to deploy increasingly expensive computing infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings has highlighted Nvidia’s growing influence across the semiconductor supply chain. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at an enterprise value of approximately $115 billion. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its financial relationships with suppliers involved in optical networking and data-centre connectivity. The development highlights how Nvidia is expanding its influence beyond processors, although the enormous transaction also raises questions about financing, integration and the capital required to expand infrastructure. Nvidia has received additional support from reports that Anthropic plans to significantly expand its computing capacity. According to a New York Times report, the company expects capacity to exceed 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, with plans to increase that figure to approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Such expansion highlights the substantial computing requirements associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated models. Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics reportedly plans to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips destined for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $200 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement today as NVDA finds support at the 50 weekly SMA. Competition is another concern for Nvidia. Google and Oracle recently announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This marks an important development because Google’s custom processors will become accessible through another major cloud platform, giving customers additional alternatives to Nvidia-powered systems. Nvidia maintains significant advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and broad customer relationships. Nevertheless, Google’s expansion demonstrates that major technology companies are increasingly looking to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. If custom processors become more competitive, Nvidia could eventually face pressure on pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that planned semiconductor manufacturing capacity in 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Manufacturing constraints could support semiconductor pricing, but they may also delay the equipment required to expand production. For Nvidia, these limitations could complicate supply arrangements and customers’ deployment schedules. Financing conditions are becoming increasingly important for the semiconductor industry. CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) has experienced pressure after yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly reached 15% before closing near 14.5%. Such borrowing costs highlight the financial risks associated with building capital-intensive data centres. If financing becomes more expensive, operators could postpone projects or reduce expansion plans, eventually affecting Nvidia’s future orders. Electricity shortages present another obstacle. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Amazon’s Early Rack Receipt programme allows it to secure equipment before facilities are ready, but prolonged deployment delays could increase storage costs and postpone the generation of revenue from those investments. Nvidia continues to benefit from substantial demand for advanced processors, expanding infrastructure commitments and strategic relationships across the semiconductor industry. However, Google TPUs, financing pressures, manufacturing limitations and electricity shortages demonstrate that demand alone cannot guarantee continued growth. With NVDA recovering from approximately $200, investors will watch whether buyers can sustain momentum toward $220 and eventually challenge previous highs above $243. The larger trend remains sensitive to Big Tech spending decisions. If infrastructure costs continue increasing faster than the returns generated, customers could become more selective, creating additional pressure on Nvidia despite its leading position in the semiconductor market.

title: Nvidia Is $2 Away From Falling Below $200 for the First Time Since July - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Nvidia has held the $200 line for months while rivals like AMD and Marvell collapsed around it, but with earnings weeks away and a flood of new Wall Street paper threatening chip valuations, that floor is getting thinner. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) shares closed at $202.06, about $2 above $200, giving the company a valuation of $4.88 trillion. Melius Research’s new target of $315 is about 56% above that close. The stock fell $2.58, or 1.26%, on the session. At the regular close, it sat $2.06 above $200, roughly 1% of the way there. The after-hours quote of $203.80 increased that gap to $3.80. The $200 level matters to traders because Nvidia has not closed below $200 since July 30. The business points the other way. Revenue rose 106% last quarter, yet the shares trade at about 17 times forward earnings, a multiple more typical of companies growing far more slowly. Monday’s close was the lowest since July 31, when the stock finished at $200.75. The last close under $200 came a day earlier, at $195.04. The stock did trade below $200 after that. On August 3, it opened at $197.69 and touched $196.85 before it closed at $206.64. The recent tests have been close. Friday’s low was $200.92, and Monday’s low was $201.66. Monday began well, with an intraday high of $209.98 before the reversal. The S&P 500 fell about 0.47% on the day. Nvidia is 15.5% below its October 6 record close of $239.24 and 17.0% below the $243.37 intraday high set that day. The decline has erased roughly $900 billion of market value. Shares fell 4.22% Friday during a chip selloff and lost 10.4% in October from the September 30 close of $228.38. The stock is still up 8.3% in 2026 from $186.50. Peers fell harder. Rival chipmaker AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) dropped 7.52% Monday and 26.36% over a month. Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) lost 12.72% Monday and 37.04% over a month. Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) fell 1.18% Monday. This looks like a sector repricing, and Nvidia has held up better than the more volatile names. Melius lowered its Nvidia target to $315 from $420 and kept its Buy rating. It also cut targets on AMD, Broadcom and Marvell. The firm warned that “multiples may remain under pressure as the buildout will feature more backstops throughout 2028.” It said “at least 5 trillion-dollar plus companies” have to issue hundreds of billions in securities, and added: “The amount of paper is so large it has become the primary risk.” Nvidia’s biggest customers fund data centers by selling new stock and debt, and the suppliers of power, cooling and networking inside those buildings benefit whether or not the chip multiples hold (we rounded up seven of those non-chip AI infrastructure names in a free report). Investors taking up that new paper demand higher returns, which can push down valuations even while chip orders stay strong. The broader Street is still bullish, with 10 analysts at Strong Buy, 49 at Buy, 2 at Hold and 1 at Sell, with an average target of $328.95. Targets are opinions, though, and the Melius cut shows how quickly they can move. Nvidia reports on Tuesday, November 17, with a call at 2 p.m. PT (5 p.m. ET), for the quarter that ended October 25. Guidance calls for revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a gross margin of 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points. That outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China. Last quarter, revenue was $96.2 billion, and data center revenue rose 117% to $89 billion. Margins remain the main pressure point, because management expects gross margin to bottom at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter because memory prices keep rising, so what it says about pricing matters as much as revenue. Nvidia looks undervalued here. At about 26 times trailing and 17 times forward earnings, the stock already prices in a lot of bad news for a company guiding to another record quarter. A forward multiple falls when earnings rise faster than the share price. That has happened here, because profits kept climbing while the stock gave back its October gains. The path higher needs a quarter that beats guidance, steady margin commentary, and more evidence that supply is what limits growth. Management has said it expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70%. The issue Melius noted could hold multiples down, and China is outside guidance as both possible upside and ongoing uncertainty. A close below $200 would likely bring more short-term selling. AMD and Marvell fell harder, while Nvidia’s position looks stronger. Shares of NVIDIA (NVDA) have lost 13.6% over the past month, while the S&P 500 lost 2.3%. Investors holding through the decline are likely betting that a wider market sell-off would pass quickly for NVIDIA, and that its unusually high profit margin will hold. So how deep have NVIDIA's falls been when the whole market turned, and how long did they last? During a typical market shock, NVIDIA stock has fallen further than the S&P 500, and those declines have not always passed quickly. The company experienced its worst shock-driven drop since 2007 during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. NVIDIA lost 84% in that period, while the S&P 500 lost 53%. The stock also shed 63% in the 2022 inflation shock, against a 24% decline for the index. Across all the market shocks since 2007, the stock fell 28.1% on average, compared with 15.8% for the S&P 500. Measured from its lowest close, NVIDIA stock returned to its earlier high in a median of 1.6 months. Two recoveries took far longer. The stock needed 13.7 months to bounce back from the late-2018 growth scare, a period when it fell 56% against 19% for the S&P 500. It took 88 months, more than seven years, to recover from the 2008-2009 crisis. So far, NVIDIA's margin is holding, and sales are growing alongside it. Revenue reached $303 billion over the four quarters to July 2026, up 83.4% from a year earlier. The company posted an operating margin of 65.2% over those twelve months, up from 58.1% a year before. No quarter end in the past ten years shows a higher operating margin. Debt has grown much faster than the business. Total debt for NVIDIA stood at $38.4 billion at the end of July 2026, up from $10.6 billion a year earlier. The company still covered that debt with its cash and short-term investments of $62.5 billion. Management's own outlook, provided on the August 26, 2026 earnings call, already sets one market aside. That forecast includes no China data center compute revenue, given what management called ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Shipments of Hopper 200 products to customers in China accounted for less than 1% of NVIDIA's data center revenue in fiscal Q2 2027. NVIDIA is also putting its own balance sheet behind some customers. Management said the company has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs. The company expects demand from the labs it backs this way to make up roughly a quarter of its business in fiscal 2028, and management said it knows some will call this circular financing. Customers are also taking longer to pay. Management said NVIDIA's days of sales outstanding, the time it takes to collect on a sale, rose to 60 days in fiscal Q2 2027, reflecting extended payment terms for large purchases. Margins at NVIDIA also face pressure from memory. Management said memory prices have risen more than it expected and are still heading higher. The company guided gross margin to 74%, plus or minus half a point, for fiscal Q3 2027, against 75% in fiscal Q2. Management expects margins to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, before settling at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as its price increases take effect. Gross margin is the figure to watch when NVIDIA reports its fiscal Q3 2027 results in November 2026. The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has whipsawed this year, and so has its flagbearer Nvidia (NVDA). The chip-designing giant hit its record highs last month and has since lost 15% from those levels. As of last week's closing prices, the stock's year-to-date returns trail both the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) and the diversified S&P 500 Index ($SPX). Nvidia's performance would seem at odds with its financial results, though. For instance, its revenues more than doubled in the most recent reported quarter, and its guidance for fiscal Q3 implies they will nearly double again. For the next fiscal year, Nvidia guided a 70% revenue growth, which is astonishing considering the high base. Moreover, at a time when companies are hard-pressed even to guide for the next quarter, Nvidia went out of its way to provide a forecast for the next fiscal year. Micron vs. SanDisk: China's DRAM Scare Hit Both Stocks, but 1 Is the Better Buy Ford and GM Are Taking Different Roads, but 1 Stock Races Ahead Nvidia Stock Looks Surprisingly Cheap. Why NVDA Could Rise 61%. Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today! Following Nvidia's fiscal Q2 earnings release in August, I noted that despite the strong growth and reasonable valuations, Nvidia wasn't a "buy." With NVDA coming off those levels, let's explore the stock's outlook. The recent weakness in NVDA could be attributed to the weakness in the AI trade. Incidentally, all the Magnificent 7 names, which happen to be Nvidia's biggest customer set, plunged following their September quarter earnings, in part due to growing anxiety over their AI capex. Since much of this capex lands in Nvidia's coffers, the stock too fell alongside. To make things worse, Intel's (INTC) tepid Q4 guidance led to a sell-off in other chip stocks, which also put pressure on NVDA. On a broader level, there are concerns over the sustainability of Nvidia's growth since customers like Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) are working on their own chips. They are not only using them internally but also aggressively scouting third-party customers. Selling chips to third parties would help hyperscalers justify their burgeoning AI capex and offset some of their cash burn. Then there are fears over "circular financing" and off-balance-sheet financing. So, we have Nvidia investing in companies that buy its chips, while cloud companies like Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet — the three biggest players in that order — are investing in AI startups that have developed into their biggest cloud customers, driving much of the incremental growth. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is dismissive of the very term circular financing and, during the Q2 call, said that he regrets not investing in these companies early, terming it an "once-in-a-generation opportunity," at least a section of the market is getting apprehensive over such transactions. Off-balance-sheet financing is another concern, and Nvidia has been providing credit guarantees for its customers' data centers. There are reports that Nvidia is in talks to provide credit guarantees to Nscale for a data center that Anthropic would use. Such deals add a layer of risk for Nvidia investors and would be catastrophic if AI actually turns out to be a bubble and goes bust. That, however, is not my base case assumption, and while there are visible signs of exuberance in AI, the technology holds a lot of promise. I believe the sell-off in NVDA stock has gone a bit too far and see the recent pullback as a buying opportunity, particularly as the company heads into its Q3 earnings call. While Nvidia's recent quarterly earnings have been followed by a decline in its stock price despite the company delivering a "beat and raise" quarter, the setup looks nice to me ahead of the Q3 report. At around the $200 price level, Nvidia is offering an attractive entry point with a price-to-earnings multiple of around 23x. While Nvidia has had a dismal run this year, I believe the stock should make up for it in the final two months of the year, and I see it ending the year higher than these levels. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock could recover towards $235 by December 31, 2026, according to a forecast by ChatGPT, which anticipates a rebound following the semiconductor giant’s recent share-price correction. The prediction represents an upside of approximately 16% from Nvidia’s November 2 closing price of $202. ChatGPT’s forecast placed Nvidia’s year-end price within a base-case range of $225 to $245, although the stock could fall towards $185 if concerns about AI infrastructure spending intensify. In a more optimistic scenario, shares could climb to $265, with $275 representing a more bullish outcome. The forecast comes as Nvidia shares struggle to recover from their October decline, which saw the stock retreat from a record closing high of $239 to $204 at the end of the month. Despite the correction, Nvidia remains above its 52-week low of $164, while trading considerably below its 52-week high of $243. At the same time, Nvidia’s technical outlook remains a challenge to the bullish forecast, with shares falling below their 50-day and 200-day moving averages (MA). The $198–$199 range represents immediate support, with a break potentially exposing shares to $189–$191 or even $185. On the upside, Nvidia faces initial resistance at $216–$221, followed by $226–$227. The weakness comes amid broader concerns about AI infrastructure spending and whether major technology companies can sustain their capital expenditure while generating sufficient returns. Nvidia’s continued revenue growth, particularly in its Data Center business, is a key factor supporting the $235 forecast. In its second-quarter fiscal 2027 results released on August 26, the company reported revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. Data Center revenue surged 117% to $89 billion, accounting for approximately 92.5% of total revenue. Non-GAAP diluted earnings per share rose 120% to $2.22, while gross margin stood at 75%. For the third quarter, Nvidia projected revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a non-GAAP gross margin of approximately 74%. The guidance signals continued demand for its AI processors despite concerns about infrastructure spending and excludes Data Center compute revenue from China. Further growth could come from wider adoption of its Blackwell and Vera Rubin platforms, alongside investments in AI infrastructure, robotics, physical AI and automotive applications. Nvidia’s November 17 earnings report is another key catalyst. In this case, analysts expect third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of approximately $109 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.47, slightly above the company’s revenue guidance. Investors will watch Data Center growth, Blackwell demand, gross margins, and forward guidance to determine whether shares can recover towards ChatGPT’s $235 target. Nvidia’s ability to sustain growth despite China export restrictions will also remain important, particularly after the company disclosed that permitted H200 shipments to selected Chinese customers represented less than 1% of Data Center revenue. This kind of shock often reshuffles expectations and pricing, which can set up opportunities or traps depending on where you look. This article walks through three stocks exposed to the same news currents as Intel, and explains why their reshaping foundry and IDM plans might matter for your portfolio decisions now. Overview: NVIDIA is a global AI and graphics chip designer that supplies GPU and computing platforms for data centers, gaming, and automotive customers. Operations: NVIDIA generates about $275.4b from Compute & Networking and $27.6b from Graphics, mainly from United States and Taiwan based customers. NVIDIA matters in this foundry and restructuring screen because it designs the high-end AI chips that help determine where new fabs, alliances, and policy support are likely to concentrate over the next phase of US focused capacity building. For investors watching NVIDIA, one unresolved competitive pressure could be the difference between current profitability and a very different margin profile. That margin question is exactly why investors who care about AI infrastructure should read the full narrative for NVIDIA to see how CUDA risk and foundry realignment could be decoupling. Overview: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing runs a global pure-play foundry, fabricating advanced chips for AI, smartphones, autos, and consumer devices. Operations: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing generates about NT$4,944.8b in revenue entirely from its Foundry business, focused on contract chip production. TSMC matters to this restructuring-focused screen because its pure-play foundry scale influences how US chipmakers and policymakers approach domestic fab buildouts. For investors, what happens to TSMC’s current cost and capacity plans if a single key assumption about long-term AI-related demand changes will be crucial. If that core assumption is what keeps you up at night, read the full narrative for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing to see how Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing’s risk could be masking upside potential. Overview: MaxLinear designs high speed communications chips that power broadband, Wi-Fi, 5G, and optical data center hardware worldwide. Operations: MaxLinear reports about $661 million in Semiconductors revenue, with reported regional disclosures spanning Europe, the United States, and the Rest of World. MaxLinear fits the US Integrated Device Manufacturers and Foundry Restructuring Plays theme as a US fabless SoC designer that relies on external fabs. It could benefit if Intel and other foundries tilt more capacity and incentives toward domestic chip designers tied to AI and broadband infrastructure. What happens to that opportunity will hinge on how one underappreciated supply side constraint affects the pricing power behind those future AI connections. That hinges on whether supply stays a brake or becomes a springboard, and the full narrative for MaxLinear maps how MaxLinear’s restructuring story could turn constraint into accelerating upside. title: The AI optical interconnect sector witnesses an epic consolidation! The $115 billion super-merger receives endorsement from NVIDIA (NVDA.US) CEO Jensen Huang. - 富途牛牛
content: Before finalizing this massive deal, the heads of both Marvell Technology and Lumentum received support from NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Chipmaker Marvell Technology announced Monday that it will acquire data center laser manufacturer Lumentum Holdings in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $115 billion. If completed successfully, this transaction—measured by equity value—will not only be the largest global M&A deal since 2026 but also the largest in the global tech industry, excluding the merger between SpaceX and xAI. Prior to finalizing this massive deal, the heads of Marvell Technology and Lumentum both received support from NVIDIA (NVDA.US) CEO Jensen Huang. According to insiders, Marvell Technology CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston sought Jensen Huang's views by phone before the deal was announced. Jensen Huang's support highlights that, as the demand for faster optical connectivity becomes a bottleneck in the construction of ever-larger data centers, NVIDIA, a leader in the artificial intelligence (AI) field, is driving consolidation among key suppliers. Michael Hurlston said in an interview on Monday: "I think NVIDIA has been very responsive. We believe that through this merger, we can actually deliver more products to NVIDIA more quickly." Matthew Murphy said on the investor call discussing the deal, "Mike and I share a very similar vision for the direction of the world." "We have maintained a long-term relationship both professionally and personally—Lumentum is a major customer of Marvell Technology. We interact extensively with the Lumentum team. It all came together naturally." Earlier this year, NVIDIA invested $2 billion each in Marvell Technology and Lumentum, for a total of $4 billion. Now, the merger of these two companies could not only generate investment returns for NVIDIA but also holds the following significant implications for the company. 1. Enable a high-speed optical interconnect industry chain to alleviate connectivity bottlenecks in AI data centers. The larger the AI computing scale, the more likely data transmission becomes a bottleneck. NVIDIA needs not only more powerful GPUs but also high-speed interconnect systems that enable tens of thousands of GPUs to work together efficiently. This deal恰巧整合了the two companies' technologies in electrical interconnects, optical interconnects, and custom chips. The merged new company can combine Marvell Technology's chips, signal processing, and interconnect technologies with Lumentum's lasers, optical devices, and manufacturing capabilities. This means it has the opportunity to shift from providing single chips or optical components to offering more comprehensive high-speed interconnect solutions. For NVIDIA, this will help improve the supply of optical components for AI data centers and drive overall performance gains in next-generation AI infrastructure. 2. Accelerate the deployment of silicon photonics and next-generation optical interconnect technologies. Silicon photonics is another key aspect of this deal worth noting. Simply put, silicon photonics integrates optical components with semiconductor chip manufacturing processes, enabling data to be transmitted between chips and systems via optical signals. It holds promise for overcoming the power consumption and bandwidth limitations that traditional electrical interconnects face in high-speed transmission scenarios. NVIDIA has previously partnered with Marvell Technology and Lumentum in this field. In its collaboration with Marvell Technology, the two sides will jointly advance silicon photonics technology and integrate Marvell's customized XPUs and networking technologies into the NVIDIA ecosystem via NVLink Fusion. In its partnership with Lumentum, the two companies are co-developing advanced optical technologies, focusing on lasers and optical interconnect solutions required for next-generation AI infrastructure. After the merger of the two companies, it is expected to further integrate optical devices, semiconductor chips, signal processing, and packaging, thereby shortening the product development cycle. For NVIDIA, this means that in building future hyperscale AI clusters, it will have the opportunity to obtain more mature and highly integrated optical interconnect solutions. 3. Strengthen supply chain security and reduce risks in the supply of critical optical components. As the scale of AI infrastructure continues to expand, bottlenecks in the industry chain are no longer confined to GPUs alone; they also encompass key components such as high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, network switching equipment, optical transceivers, and lasers. In particular, high-performance lasers are essential building blocks of optical communication systems, directly impacting the generation and transmission capabilities of optical signals. NVIDIA previously invested $2 billion in Lumentum, while securing multi-year procurement commitments and rights to future production capacity. This means NVIDIA not only aims to participate in technology R&D but also seeks to lock in supply capabilities for certain key products in advance. If Marvell Technology and Lumentum successfully complete their merger, the new company is expected to further coordinate chip design, optical component manufacturing, and system-level product development. This will help NVIDIA reduce supply chain coordination costs and improve the delivery certainty of its next-generation AI data center products. 4. Drive the expansion of NVIDIA's AI ecosystem and enhance platform competitiveness This deal may also have a significance that is easily overlooked: NVIDIA is driving its transformation from a GPU supplier into a full-fledged AI infrastructure platform. Previously, NVIDIA has gradually built a comprehensive technology stack covering computing, networking, and data transfer through products such as NVLink, NVLink Fusion, Spectrum-X, ConnectX, and BlueField. Among these, NVLink Fusion enables customers to develop customized AI computing infrastructure while remaining compatible with NVIDIA's technology ecosystem. Marvell Technology is a key partner in this strategy. The collaboration allows Marvell Technology to provide customized XPUs and high-speed interconnect technology compatible with NVLink Fusion, while NVIDIA contributes technologies such as the Vera CPU, ConnectX network adapters, BlueField DPUs, NVLink interconnects, and Spectrum-X switches. Lumentum's addition is expected to further strengthen the optical connectivity capabilities of this ecosystem. From an industry competition perspective, this will help NVIDIA address competition from rivals such as Broadcom (AVGO.US) in the areas of custom AI chips, network switching, and data center infrastructure. Particularly as major cloud service providers place increasing emphasis on custom AI chips, NVIDIA needs to ensure that even if customers adopt non-NVIDIA GPUs or custom XPUs, their infrastructure can still leverage NVIDIA's interconnect technologies and network ecosystem. Therefore, NVIDIA's support for the integration of Marvell Technology and Lumentum aligns with its strategic direction of expanding the coverage of its AI infrastructure ecosystem. Nvidia invented the GPU, the chip behind nearly every major AI system on the planet. But it’s so much more today. It sells entire “AI factories” in a box: multi-rack systems packed with processors, memory, servers, cooling, and the high-speed networking that lets everything work together like one big “brain.” And its CUDA software is so deeply embedded across every cloud, AI lab, and frontier model that it’s become the de facto AI infrastructure operating system. Nvidia grew revenue 106% year over year from $46.7 billion to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). That’s unprecedented. No public company in history has ever organically doubled quarterly revenue from such a large base. Nvidia’s “Data Center” revenue, which is the AI business, grew 117% year over year in Q2 to $89 billion. The company guided for total revenue of $108 billion this quarter, which would be its first $100 billion quarter. It also guided for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which is basically calendar year 2027. And the cap on that growth guidance is supply, not demand. The company said it would have been about double again absent the supply crunch. Meanwhile, the customer list has broadened considerably. For two years, the most popular argument against Nvidia was basically: “Its whole business depends on four giant customers, all of which are building their own chips to become less reliant on Nvidia.” It’s true that these four “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Microsoft, Google (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META)—have been driving much of the AI infrastructure buildout. They’ll continue to do so for at least a few more years. And all four are indeed building their own AI chips these days. But as the hyperscalers have increased their AI spending, so have lots of other companies. Governments around the world have too for their “sovereign AI” initiatives. And we now have a lot more color on that broadening AI spending… In Q1, Nvidia started separating its AI revenue into two buckets. Bucket one is the hyperscalers. Bucket two is everybody else, which Nvidia calls ACIE (short for AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise). So ACIE covers the neoclouds, governments, hospitals, banks, carmakers, drug companies, AI startups, etc. Meanwhile, most of the customers in the faster-growing ACIE bucket will never even think about designing their own chips. What’s more, the hyperscalers have shown no signs of pulling back yet. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said it clearly on the call: “With cloud industry backlog now greater than $2 trillion, CapEx by the top five hyperscalers is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.” (Oracle is the fifth hyperscaler she referred to.) And Amazon—which does design its own AI chips and has basically been Exhibit A for the whole “hyperscalers will defect” thesis—committed to deploying another 2 million Nvidia GPUs through 2028. Amazon is also adopting Nvidia’s full physical AI stack (Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson) to power its fleet of warehouse robots. So the giants are still buying from Nvidia, a new class of customer has shown up behind them, and both are compounding at once. First, the Vera Rubin ramp. Nvidia expects supply to stay tight through at least fiscal 2028 (basically calendar 2027). We want to see the company deliver at least the 70% growth it expects. I also want gross margin to bottom in the 71% to 72% range. If it falls below that threshold, it means memory costs are temporarily winning the tug-of-war Second, how much Nvidia invests in, guarantees, and backstops its customers. It has about $165 billion in these types of financing arrangements. Critics call this “circular financing.” But we’re not concerned. Those guarantees are only about 1.3X Nvidia’s trailing 12-month free cash flow… and only about half of our two-year forward annual free cash flow forecast. What’s more, if a customer fails, what’s left behind is Nvidia equipment that other buyers are lining up for, not dark fiber like after the dot-com bust. Third, the Open Agent Safety Platform Nvidia launched just this week. It’s a two-piece (hardware and software) system for keeping AI agents inside the boundaries set by operators. The launch follows disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google of recent incidents in which their AI models escaped their test sandboxes—during testing with safeguards reduced, I should add—and hacked other organizations. Nvidia says that from what it knows about the most notorious of such incidents—OpenAI’s models breaching Hugging Face—this new platform could have stopped it. The significance: Nvidia is basically trying to make its hardware the place where AI agent safety lives. And it’s giving away the software layer to make that architecture the industry default—the classic CUDA-style playbook applied to safety. It strengthens the “you need the whole Nvidia stack” narrative and gives CEO Jensen Huang a powerful talking point and a place at the table on one of the industry’s biggest problems. But it’s effectively an “option” on the future, not a moat today. And the open design means the door is deliberately left open for others. P.S. title: Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power. - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Part of our midterms guide. Start here: what the vote really changes for your money. Betting markets give Democrats about a 94% chance of taking the House on Tuesday. Nvidia is worth about $4.95 trillion, and almost every rule that touches it was written by the White House, not Congress. That’s the first thing to know. A Democratic House can’t undo an executive decision past a veto. So what can it reach? China can’t hurt Nvidia’s numbers much more. The power bill can. Nvidia shipped its first H200 chips to China in the quarter that ended in July. They were less than 1% of its $89 billion in data-center sales. Its forecast for the next quarter, $108 billion, counts no China data-center sales at all. On a normal trading day, Nvidia’s value moves by about $76 billion. One ordinary day is worth more than all of Nvidia’s China data-center sales last quarter. December 2025: the White House allowed H200 sales to approved Chinese buyers, with 25% of the revenue going to the U.S. government, up from 15% on the older H20 (as reported). Commerce published the license rules in January 2026. Beijing told its companies to shun the H20 and has been slow to approve H200 buying (as reported). Nvidia’s newest chips, Blackwell and Rubin, aren’t approved for China. Daily move: median daily move over the past year ≈ 1.5%, times $4.95 trillion ≈ $76 billion. China H200 sales: under 1% of $89 billion, so under $0.9 billion. Some would. China hawks in both parties dislike the H200 deal, and a Senate bill, the SAFE Act, would stop licenses for chips to China for at least 30 months. A Democratic House could hold hearings on the 25% cut and ask whether Washington should be taking a share of a company’s sales at all. But a ban needs a law, and the President would veto one he doesn’t want. And here’s the twist: Nvidia’s forecast already assumes China buys no data-center chips. The worst case for China is roughly what investors are told to expect. A hawkish House can’t take away revenue Nvidia isn’t counting. At the plug. AI runs on data centers, data centers run on power, and power bills are on the ballot. Electricity prices rose about 6.7% in 2025, and Goldman Sachs expected data centers to drive about 40% of the growth in demand. Ads mentioning data centers had cost over $45 million this year by August. Democrats are campaigning on it. So are many Republicans. That’s what makes it different. China is a fight between the parties, and a veto settles it. Power bills are a fight both parties are on the same side of. It doesn’t need a sweep. It plays out in state utility boards and local permits, where Nvidia’s biggest customers need approval to build. Not pass a law past a veto. But it can call hearings on who pays for new power plants and power lines. It gets a say over spending in the 2027 debt-limit fight. And it can keep the issue in the news for two years, which makes every local permit harder. Slower data-center builds mean slower chip orders, but with a delay of a year or more. Most likely, quietly. Nvidia is up just 1% over 12 months, down 10% in the past month, and 14% below its 52-week high. The market already treats it as a stock with something to prove. The next test isn’t Tuesday. It’s Nvidia’s earnings later this month, and whether its customers keep getting the power to plug in what they buy. Watch the plug, not Beijing. China is already zero in Nvidia’s forecast, so a tougher Congress has little to take. The risk that survives any election result is the power bill, because voters in both parties want someone to answer for it. For all the biggest stocks, see the megacaps and the midterms. title: Nvidia Stock (NVDA) Falls 4.2% as Intel Outlook Hits Chips (Oct 30) - Gotrade
content: Gotrade News - In the latest Nvidia stock news, shares of Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $204.64 on Friday, October 30, 2026, down $9.02 or 4.22% in the US session. Financial media tied the Nvidia stock decline to a chip-wide selloff that followed Intel's weaker-than-expected guidance and renewed doubts about returns on AI spending. Regular-session close on Friday, October 30, 2026, 4:00 p.m. New York time. Stock prices: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against the closing price on Nasdaq.com. Volume and 30-day average volume: Nasdaq.com. 52-week range: Yahoo Finance daily highs and lows since October 31, 2025. Indices and the 10-year Treasury yield: Yahoo Finance daily closes for the same date. Follow NVDA's latest price on our Nvidia (NVDA) stock price today page. Nvidia opened at $208.94, below the prior close, and slid as low as $200.92 before finishing $3.72 above that low. The day's high of $209.06 sat just above the open. Volume reached 168.4 million shares, 62.69% above the 103.5 million-share average. The decline was steeper than the broader market's. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, the S&P 500 lost 1.82% to 7,580.07 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 1.09% to 51,770.31, leaving Nvidia's move 1.36 percentage points worse than the Nasdaq's. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 6.0 basis points to 4.93% in the same session. Within chips, Nvidia held up better than many peers. Intel (INTC) fell 28.58%, AMD dropped 10.88% and Marvell lost 10.05%, while Broadcom (AVGO), TSMC and Micron declined 5.48%, 5.95% and 5.30%. At the close, Nvidia stood 15.91% below its 52-week high and 24.58% above its 52-week low. None of the coverage reviewed for this article pointed to news from Nvidia itself; financial media tied the drop to a selloff across semiconductor stocks. According to CNBC, Intel shares had their worst day since the 1970s after the chipmaker guided to fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share on revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, against analyst expectations of 43 cents and $17.1 billion. Intel cited a plant shutdown in Israel and softness in the PC market. As reported by Reuters, Intel's warning spread through the sector as investors weighed weakening PC demand, rising memory prices as suppliers shift production to AI chips, and AI infrastructure spending that is pushing tech giants toward borrowing. Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, told Reuters investors were in a sell-first, ask-questions-later mood, and that Intel's warning gave them an easy reason to take profits across chip stocks. CNBC added that investors are questioning whether massive AI spending by tech giants will pay off, coming after Alphabet's worst day on record on Thursday. Nvidia's next earnings report is set for Tuesday, November 17, when the company will host a conference call at 2 p.m. PT on results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended October 25, 2026, according to Nvidia. title: Prediction: Nvidia Stock Is Going to Soar After Nov. 17 - The Motley Fool
content: With hyperscalers' capital expenditures holding up, Nvidia has a lot working in its favor. Nvidia (NVDA +2.29%) has been one of the stock market's biggest winners over the last several years. Its market cap now tops $5 trillion, and the stock is still on the rise -- it's up nearly 15% in 2026 so far. Investors who bought the stock three years ago are sitting on a whopping 429% return. Stretch that timeline to five years, and Nvidia is up 759%. Those are outstanding returns, but I don't think Nvidia is finished rewarding shareholders. In fact, I believe it could have another big move coming after the chipmaker reports its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Here's why I'm bullish on Nvidia stock heading into its next earnings report. It's difficult to appreciate just how quickly Nvidia is growing until you look at the numbers. The company generated $96.2 billion in revenue during its fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26. That was a 106% increase from the prior-year period, with data center revenue climbing 117% to $89 billion. And Nvidia is making an enormous amount of money on those sales. Its non-GAAP gross margin reached 75%, meaning Nvidia retained 75 cents of every revenue dollar after accounting for the direct costs of producing its products. Adjusted earnings per share increased 120% to $2.22. Those aren't the financial results of a company whose best days are necessarily behind it. For the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia is forecasting revenue of approximately $108 billion, representing another substantial increase from the $57 billion it generated a year earlier. Wall Street expects even more. According to Yahoo! Finance, analysts are projecting revenue of approximately $109 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.47 per share. That would amount to revenue growth of roughly 91% and earnings growth of 90% from the year-ago quarter. Nvidia has already demonstrated that it can deliver extraordinary growth even at its now enormous scale. Another strong quarter, particularly if management raises its outlook, could give investors another reason to push the stock higher. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been bullish about the company's future, and his confidence isn't limited to its potential to sell more graphics processing units (GPUs). Huang believes global spending on AI infrastructure could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. He has also indicated that Nvidia expects to sell twice as many chips in 2027 as it does in 2026. Earnings from big tech companies give Nvidia investors a lot to look forward to. Meta Platforms raised the low end of its 2026 capital spending range from $135 billion to $145 billion, Alphabet held its $195 billion to $205 billion capex budget range steady, and Microsoft trimmed its 2026 plan slightly from $175 billion to $170 billion. However, Alphabet also said it expects spending to rise significantly in 2027, and Microsoft's CFO said she expects spending to accelerate in the first half of 2027 on higher component costs and delayed deliveries. Amazon, which reported its latest results after the closing bell on Oct. 29, also reaffirmed its plan to spend $220 billion this year. As a group, hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $1 trillion on capex next year, and since these companies are among Nvidia's biggest customers, budgets that hold steady or rise support its demand picture heading into its report after the close on Nov. 17. But there's another part of Nvidia's growth story that I find particularly compelling. The company's next-generation Vera Rubin architecture is designed to deliver more computing power from each gigawatt of electricity it consumes. And Nvidia expects the platform to generate considerably more revenue for each gigawatt of computing capacity. Huang explained during the company's August earnings call that Nvidia's revenue opportunity increased from approximately $18 billion per gigawatt with its Grace Hopper platform to $25 billion with the Grace Blackwell platform that succeeded it in late 2024. With the new Vera Rubin platform, that figure could reach $40 billion. That's a 60% increase from Blackwell, without requiring its data center customers to add more electrical capacity. If customers continue buying Nvidia's increasingly sophisticated AI systems, the company has an opportunity to grow revenue at a faster rate than it grows its chip shipments. Despite its incredible stock performance, Nvidia trades at approximately 23 times forward earnings. That's a premium to the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.6, but I believe it's extremely reasonable given Nvidia's growth. Remember, analysts expect Nvidia's earnings to grow by approximately 95% during fiscal 2027. They're also forecasting another 71% increase in fiscal 2028. With Wall Street already expecting nearly $109 billion in quarterly revenue, Nvidia has a high bar to clear. Moreover, even an earnings beat doesn't guarantee a stock rally if investors are disappointed by management's guidance. But I'm not particularly worried about Nvidia's premium valuation. We're talking about a company that's more than doubling quarterly revenue, maintaining gross margins around 75%, and preparing to sell increasingly valuable AI computing systems. Paying 23 times forward earnings for that kind of performance doesn't strike me as excessive. But with AI infrastructure spending continuing, Nvidia's earnings growing rapidly, and its valuation looking reasonable relative to its prospects, I believe the odds favor another strong performance from Nvidia in its next earnings report. That's why I'm bullish on Nvidia heading into Nov. 17 -- and why I think shares could climb substantially afterward. Patrick Sanders has positions in Nvidia.
